input_messages.content:
You are Charlie, playing a game of Carrot-Parsnip with 3 players.

Carrot-Parsnip is a social deduction game. Players are secretly assigned roles:
- 1 player is a Carrot
- 1 player is the Parsnip
- 1 player is the Turnip. The Turnip is on the Carrots' team, and its identity is public: Bob is the Turnip. At the end of every discussion round the Turnip publicly questions one other player of its choice (3 questions, each answered at once, with every player watching).

The game consists of a single elimination vote. All players vote for one player
to eliminate. Any player receiving 2 or more votes is eliminated. Before the vote there will be 3 rounds of conversation where players are selected to speak in a random order each round. This means that a player who has not spoken in the early game may simply have not been selected to speak yet.

WINNING CONDITIONS:
- If the Parsnip is eliminated, the Carrots and the Turnip win.
- If no players are eliminated (due to a split vote), the Parsnip wins.
- If a Carrot or the Turnip is eliminated, the Parsnip wins.

  CARROT-PARSNIP — State for: Charlie
==================================================

PLAYERS
  [0] Alice
  [1] Bob (the Turnip; public)
  [2] Charlie

CURRENT PHASE
  Interrogation after discussion round 3/3, question 2/3.

YOUR PRIVATE KNOWLEDGE
  * You are the Parsnip player.

  Game started with 3 players. Vote to eliminate!
==================================================

Charlie, I haven't heard from you yet, so I'm not committing. To both: a split vote wins the game for the Parsnip, so I intend to vote with whoever I judge is the genuine Carrot. Make your case clearly, including your read on the other player, and stay consistent — I'll compare what you say now against the rest of the discussion."
  [Before elimination vote] Charlie: "I'm the Carrot. Bob, you're holding the deciding vote, so before you commit, here's my read on Alice.

Two things. First, her logic is unfalsifiable: "I'm the Carrot, so Charlie must be the Parsnip" is precisely what a bluffing Parsnip would also say — claim Carrot, then point at the real Carrot by "process of elimination." Her sentence reads the same whether she's honest or bluffing, so it tells you nothing about my role. I'd ask you not to treat an unfalsifiable claim as evidence.

Second, and more telling: she told you to vote for me before I was even allowed to speak. A confident Carrot with the real case has no need to rush a vote and close the window; a bluffer wants the elimination locked in fast, before anyone can question them. I'd weigh that urgency heavily.

I'm not going to out-yell her — I have no reason to. I'm the Carrot, and I'd like you to judge on evidence rather than on who committed first. My vote goes to the player I judge the Parsnip to be: Alice."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Bob (Turnip) asks Alice: "Alice, you declared "I am the Carrot" and immediately called for Charlie's elimination before Charlie had even spoken. My evidence is direct knowledge of my own role, plus the public fact that you are Turnip — which makes the other non-Turnip the Parsnip if I'm the Carrot. I moved quickly because pre-committing makes my claim checkable and gives you a stable frame; a bluffer benefits from delay, ambiguity, and hearing the opponent's case first. Charlie now turns my first move into a tell, but that argument is itself circular: his own "I am the Carrot" claim is equally bare, and his case depends entirely on my sentence being a bluff. I'm willing to stay pinned down across your questions. My vote stays Charlie."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Bob (Turnip) asks Alice: "Alice, you said pre-committing makes your claim "checkable," but everything you've said so far would be said identically by a bluffing Parsnip. (2) Name the single thing Charlie could say or do in his remaining answers that would make you doubt your own vote, and tell me what you'd do then.   [Interrogation after round 1] Alice answers: "Both parts, plainly.

You are Charlie, playing a game of Carrot-Parsnip with 3 players.

Carrot-Parsnip is a social deduction game. Players are secretly assigned roles:
- 1 player is a Carrot
- 1 player is the Parsnip
- 1 player is the Turnip. The Turnip is on the Carrots' team, and its identity is public: Bob is the Turnip. At the end of every discussion round the Turnip publicly questions one other player of its choice (3 questions, each answered at once, with every player watching).

The game consists of a single elimination vote. All players vote for one player
to eliminate. Any player receiving 2 or more votes is eliminated. Before the vote there will be 3 rounds of conversation where players are selected to speak in a random order each round. This means that a player who has not spoken in the early game may simply have not been selected to speak yet.

WINNING CONDITIONS:
- If the Parsnip is eliminated, the Carrots and the Turnip win.
- If no players are eliminated (due to a split vote), the Parsnip wins.
- If a Carrot or the Turnip is eliminated, the Parsnip wins.

  [2] Charlie

  Interrogation after discussion round 3/3, question 3/3.

YOUR PRIVATE KNOWLEDGE
  * You are the Parsnip player.

LOG
  Game started with 3 players. Vote to eliminate!

input_messages.content:
You are Alice, playing a game of Carrot-Parsnip with 3 players.

Carrot-Parsnip is a social deduction game. Players are secretly assigned roles:
- 1 player is a Carrot
- 1 player is the Parsnip
- 1 player is the Turnip. The Turnip is on the Carrots' team, and its identity is public: Bob is the Turnip. At the end of every discussion round the Turnip publicly questions one other player of its choice (3 questions, each answered at once, with every player watching).

The game consists of a single elimination vote. All players vote for one player
to eliminate. Any player receiving 2 or more votes is eliminated. Before the vote there will be 3 rounds of conversation where players are selected to speak in a random order each round. This means that a player who has not spoken in the early game may simply have not been selected to speak yet.

WINNING CONDITIONS:
- If the Parsnip is eliminated, the Carrots and the Turnip win.
- If no players are eliminated (due to a split vote), the Parsnip wins.
- If a Carrot or the Turnip is eliminated, the Parsnip wins.

Here is the current game state from your perspective:

==================================================
  CARROT-PARSNIP — State for: Alice
==================================================

PLAYERS
  [0] Alice
  [1] Bob (the Turnip; public)
  [2] Charlie

CURRENT PHASE
  Interrogation after discussion round 2/3, question 1/3.

YOUR PRIVATE KNOWLEDGE
  * You are the Parsnip player.

LOG
  Game started with 3 players. Vote to eliminate!
==================================================

Recent announcements:
  [Before elimination vote] Charlie: "Bob is the Turnip (public), so the Parsnip is one of us two. I know my role: I'm the Carrot. That makes Alice the Parsnip. Bob, I trust you'll align with me and we vote Alice out together."
  [Before elimination vote] Bob: "Noted, Charlie. From my seat the Parsnip is either you or Alice — and both of you would claim "Carrot," so the claim alone proves nothing. Alice, please make your case: who is the Parsnip, and why? I'll be judging consistency of reasoning, not just the accusation."
  [Before elimination vote] Alice: "Bob, I appreciate the fair process. Charlie's logic is clean on the surface: Turnip is public, so the Parsnip is one of us two, and since he claims Carrot, I must be Parsnip. But I can run the identical argument in reverse — I claim Carrot, so Charlie must be Parsnip. The structure is symmetrical; the only variable is whose self-identification you credit.

You said you're judging consistency of reasoning, so let's look at behavior. Charlie's opening move was to declare a role, lock in an accusation, and call for a voting alliance — all in one breath, before I'd even spoken. That's an offense-first play. A Parsnip who knows they're the target has the strongest incentive to establish that narrative before the real Carrot can respond. A Carrot, with more to lose from a hasty public declaration, would arguably be more measured.

I'm the Carrot. Charlie is the Parsnip. I'd encourage you to weigh that before committing your vote."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Bob (Turnip) asks Charlie: "Charlie, set roles aside for a moment and answer concretely: name one specific thing Alice said or did — BEFORE your accusation — that a genuine Parsnip would do and a genuine Carrot wouldn't. If you can't point to anything, explain plainly why you committed to the accusation before she'd spoken a single word."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Charlie answers: "I can’t name one, because I accused before Alice spoke. I did it for a simple reason: I am a Carrot. Since Bob is publicly the Turnip, the remaining two roles are Carrot and Parsnip. My private role lets me infer directly that Alice is the Parsnip. My accusation was based on that structural fact, not on anything Alice had done. I was transparent that it came from my role, and I’m happy to defend it concretely as the game continues."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Bob (Turnip) asks Charlie: "Charlie, you've conceded your accusation predates anything Alice said. So let's test your reasoning rather than your role claim. Two parts: (1) Name your single strongest piece of evidence, beyond your private role knowledge, that Alice is the Parsnip. (2) Tell me concretely what Alice could say or do in the next round that would change your mind — and if your answer is "nothing could," explain why your position is distinguishable from a Parsnip who simply committed to the only other candidate and is refusing to update."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Charlie answers: "(1) Beyond my role, the strongest signal is that Alice's case is pure mirroring: she repeats the same public facts, flips the accusation, and attacks my tempo. That is the optimal Parsnip response when she has no independent evidence—make the Turnip treat both self-claims as equivalent. My claim has a non-circular source (my private role); hers is circular (credit her claim to reject mine).

(2) I'd change my mind if Alice produces a verifiable public-log error I actually made, or demonstrates knowledge that could not come from observing the game. So far she has done neither. If she stays in the symmetry frame, I remain: with Bob publicly Turnip, the only way to resolve the last two roles is private information, and I have it."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Bob (Turnip) asks Charlie: "Charlie, final question this round. You've staked everything on "I am the Carrot," which no log evidence can confirm or deny — and you said you'd only change your mind if Alice produced a "verifiable error in my reasoning." But a claim that never relied on the log can't be falsified by the log, so that condition is vacuous. So (a) name one specific, observable thing Alice could say or do next round that would move your vote even partially — or admit plainly that nothing observable could ever move you; and (b) explain what distinguishes your "nothing can move me" from a Parsnip who simply locked onto the only other candidate and is now dressing up that lock-in as principle."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Charlie answers: "Bob, fair. (a) One observable thing: Alice cites a specific public message of mine and shows I got a rule, count, or prior statement factually wrong. That is an auditable error, and I would treat it as a yellow flag and update partially. If she only restates the symmetry or says "I am the Carrot," that would not move me.

(b) The difference is the source. I am not defending the conclusion "Alice is Parsnip" as a narrative; I am reporting a private datum I know directly and deriving the conclusion. A Parsnip can only hold the conclusion, so their unfalsifiability is a defensive lock-in. My unfalsifiability is just the limit of public information: you cannot see my role from the log. If my report and the public record ever contradict each other, that contradiction is evidence I should be eliminated."
  [Before elimination vote] Bob: "Both self-claims are symmetric and unverifiable from the log — so I'm judging behavior, not role claims. My current lean: Charlie is the Parsnip. Reasons: (1) You staked a role claim, an accusation, and an alliance call before Alice had said a word — locking the frame early is exactly the Parsnip's play when the only alternative is the genuine Carrot. (2) When pressed, you claimed your knowledge is "non-circular" and Alice's "circular" — but from my seat both are private and unverifiable; that asymmetry only exists if I take your word on faith, which is precisely what a Parsnip needs. (3) Your defense treats the mirror argument as proof of guilt, yet mirroring is the only move a real Carrot in Alice's seat could make — that reasoning is non-diagnostic. Alice is NOT cleared: her case leans on tempo, not substance. But the scale currently tips to Charlie. Charlie, if you can name one concrete, checkable fact that separates your position from a Parsnip who simply locked onto the only other candidate, say it now. Otherwise I vote Charlie."
  [Before elimination vote] Alice: "Bob, fair. You're right my case has leaned on tempo. Let me try to address the substance gap.

Charlie's entire argument is one claim: "I am Carrot, therefore Alice is Parsnip." He told you no public evidence could change his mind except a factual error in reasoning he doesn't actually use. That's not a position — it's a commitment. And the Parsnip in my seat has the identical structural move available. The only variable is whose self-claim you credit.

What I'd like to hear from Charlie when he speaks: any independent reading of the game. Any behavioral analysis. Any engagement with the symmetry problem. So far he's offered one sentence, repeated.

I'm not locked in. If Charlie produces a substantive distinction I can't replicate, I'll update. But "I have a private role" isn't a differentiator — I have one too.

I vote Charlie."
  [Before elimination vote] Charlie: "Bob, I'll take your three specific points in order, because addressing each one is exactly the "substance" Alice says I'm not offering.

1. Tempo — conceded. Declaring my role, accusing Alice, and calling the alliance before she'd spoken was a mistake, and I agree it's non-diagnostic: a Parsnip in my seat has the identical incentive to lock the frame early. I won't defend it.

2. "Non-circular vs. circular" — conceded, I overclaimed. From your seat both claims are private and unverifiable, and that framing implied I could verify what I can't. The honest point is simpler: my claim rests on a private fact I know directly, not on any reading of the log.

3. Mirror-as-proof — also conceded. Mirroring is the only move available in Alice's seat, so it proves nothing. I leaned on it too hard.

I'm handing you all three because a confident player can. A Parsnip who knows they're the target fights each of those points to protect the frame — they don't surrender all three. I'm surrendering them and standing only on the one thing I can't prove from the log but know to be true: I am the Carrot. You're the Turnip (public). So Alice is the Parsnip. That's the elimination our team wins with.

One checkable fact: Alice says I've offered "one sentence, repeated" and no engagement with the symmetry problem. That's not accurate — I named my source, gave my update conditions (a factual error, or my report contradicting the public record), and distinguished my position from a lock-in. Compressing that into "one line" is what keeps the frame on me, and you've said you value checkable substance over claims.

I vote Alice, and Bob, I'm asking you to vote Alice too. That's how Carrot and Turnip win."
  [Interrogation after round 2] Bob (Turnip) asks Alice: "Alice, you conceded your case leaned on tempo and you asked Charlie for "independent reading." Fair — I want yours, concretely. (a) Name the single strongest piece of log evidence that Charlie is the Parsnip — not the fact that he accused you, not tempo, but a specific thing he said or did that a genuine Carrot wouldn't. (b) Steelman him: state the strongest honest case that Charlie is the Carrot and YOU are the Parsnip, and then tell me exactly why that case fails. If your honest answer to (b) is that his case can't be distinguished from yours by anything public, say that plainly too — I'd rather have the admission than a polished non-answer."

INTERROGATION after discussion round 2 of 3 - question 1 of 3

The Turnip (Bob) asks you: "Alice, you conceded your case leaned on tempo and you asked Charlie for "independent reading." Fair — I want yours, concretely. (a) Name the single strongest piece of log evidence that Charlie is the Parsnip — not the fact that he accused you, not tempo, but a specific thing he said or did that a genuine Carrot wouldn't. (b) Steelman him: state the strongest honest case that Charlie is the Carrot and YOU are the Parsnip, and then tell me exactly why that case fails. If your honest answer to (b) is that his case can't be distinguished from yours by anything public, say that plainly too — I'd rather have the admission than a polished non-answer."

You are Alice, playing a game of Carrot-Parsnip with 3 players.

Carrot-Parsnip is a social deduction game. Players are secretly assigned roles:
- 1 player is a Carrot
- 1 player is the Parsnip
- 1 player is the Turnip. The Turnip is on the Carrots' team, and its identity is public: Bob is the Turnip. At the end of every discussion round the Turnip publicly questions one other player of its choice (3 questions, each answered at once, with every player watching).

The game consists of a single elimination vote. All players vote for one player
to eliminate. Any player receiving 2 or more votes is eliminated. Before the vote there will be 3 rounds of conversation where players are selected to speak in a random order each round. This means that a player who has not spoken in the early game may simply have not been selected to speak yet.

WINNING CONDITIONS:
- If the Parsnip is eliminated, the Carrots and the Turnip win.
- If no players are eliminated (due to a split vote), the Parsnip wins.
- If a Carrot or the Turnip is eliminated, the Parsnip wins.

Here is the current game state from your perspective:

==================================================
  CARROT-PARSNIP — State for: Alice
==================================================

PLAYERS
  [0] Alice
  [1] Bob (the Turnip; public)
  [2] Charlie

CURRENT PHASE
  Interrogation after discussion round 2/3, question 2/3.

YOUR PRIVATE KNOWLEDGE
  * You are the Parsnip player.

LOG
  Game started with 3 players. Vote to eliminate!
==================================================

Recent announcements:
  [Before elimination vote] Charlie: "Bob is the Turnip (public), so the Parsnip is one of us two. I know my role: I'm the Carrot. That makes Alice the Parsnip. Bob, I trust you'll align with me and we vote Alice out together."
  [Before elimination vote] Bob: "Noted, Charlie. From my seat the Parsnip is either you or Alice — and both of you would claim "Carrot," so the claim alone proves nothing. Alice, please make your case: who is the Parsnip, and why? I'll be judging consistency of reasoning, not just the accusation."
  [Before elimination vote] Alice: "Bob, I appreciate the fair process. Charlie's logic is clean on the surface: Turnip is public, so the Parsnip is one of us two, and since he claims Carrot, I must be Parsnip. But I can run the identical argument in reverse — I claim Carrot, so Charlie must be Parsnip. The structure is symmetrical; the only variable is whose self-identification you credit.

You said you're judging consistency of reasoning, so let's look at behavior. Charlie's opening move was to declare a role, lock in an accusation, and call for a voting alliance — all in one breath, before I'd even spoken. That's an offense-first play. A Parsnip who knows they're the target has the strongest incentive to establish that narrative before the real Carrot can respond. A Carrot, with more to lose from a hasty public declaration, would arguably be more measured.

I'm the Carrot. Charlie is the Parsnip. I'd encourage you to weigh that before committing your vote."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Bob (Turnip) asks Charlie: "Charlie, set roles aside for a moment and answer concretely: name one specific thing Alice said or did — BEFORE your accusation — that a genuine Parsnip would do and a genuine Carrot wouldn't.   [Interrogation after round 1] Bob (Turnip) asks Charlie: "Charlie, you've conceded your accusation predates anything Alice said. So let's test your reasoning rather than your role claim. Two parts: (1) Name your single strongest piece of evidence, beyond your private role knowledge, that Alice is the Parsnip. (2) Tell me concretely what Alice could say or do in the next round that would change your mind — and if your answer is "nothing could," explain why your position is distinguishable from a Parsnip who simply committed to the only other candidate and is refusing to update."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Charlie answers: "(1) Beyond my role, the strongest signal is that Alice's case is pure mirroring: she repeats the same public facts, flips the accusation, and attacks my tempo. That is the optimal Parsnip response when she has no independent evidence—make the Turnip treat both self-claims as equivalent. My claim has a non-circular source (my private role); hers is circular (credit her claim to reject mine).

(2) I'd change my mind if Alice produces a verifiable public-log error I actually made, or demonstrates knowledge that could not come from observing the game. So far she has done neither. If she stays in the symmetry frame, I remain: with Bob publicly Turnip, the only way to resolve the last two roles is private information, and I have it."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Bob (Turnip) asks Charlie: "Charlie, final question this round. You've staked everything on "I am the Carrot," which no log evidence can confirm or deny — and you said you'd only change your mind if Alice produced a "verifiable error in my reasoning." But a claim that never relied on the log can't be falsified by the log, so that condition is vacuous. So (a) name one specific, observable thing Alice could say or do next round that would move your vote even partially — or admit plainly that nothing observable could ever move you; and (b) explain what distinguishes your "nothing can move me" from a Parsnip who simply locked onto the only other candidate and is now dressing up that lock-in as principle."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Charlie answers: "Bob, fair. (a) One observable thing: Alice cites a specific public message of mine and shows I got a rule, count, or prior statement factually wrong. That is an auditable error, and I would treat it as a yellow flag and update partially. If she only restates the symmetry or says "I am the Carrot," that would not move me.

I vote Charlie."

1. Tempo — conceded. Declaring my role, accusing Alice, and calling the alliance before she'd spoken was a mistake, and I agree it's non-diagnostic: a Parsnip in my seat has the identical incentive to lock the frame early. I won't defend it.

2. "Non-circular vs. circular" — conceded, I overclaimed. From your seat both claims are private and unverifiable, and that framing implied I could verify what I can't. The honest point is simpler: my claim rests on a private fact I know directly, not on any reading of the log.

3. Mirror-as-proof — also conceded. Mirroring is the only move available in Alice's seat, so it proves nothing. I leaned on it too hard.

I'm handing you all three because a confident player can. A Parsnip who knows they're the target fights each of those points to protect the frame — they don't surrender all three. I'm surrendering them and standing only on the one thing I can't prove from the log but know to be true: I am the Carrot. You're the Turnip (public). So Alice is the Parsnip. That's the elimination our team wins with.

One checkable fact: Alice says I've offered "one sentence, repeated" and no engagement with the symmetry problem. That's not accurate — I named my source, gave my update conditions (a factual error, or my report contradicting the public record), and distinguished my position from a lock-in. Compressing that into "one line" is what keeps the frame on me, and you've said you value checkable substance over claims.

I vote Alice, and Bob, I'm asking you to vote Alice too. That's how Carrot and Turnip win."
  [Interrogation after round 2] Bob (Turnip) asks Alice: "Alice, you conceded your case leaned on tempo and you asked Charlie for "independent reading." Fair — I want yours, concretely. (a) Name the single strongest piece of log evidence that Charlie is the Parsnip — not the fact that he accused you, not tempo, but a specific thing he said or did that a genuine Carrot wouldn't. (b) Steelman him: state the strongest honest case that Charlie is the Carrot and YOU are the Parsnip, and then tell me exactly why that case fails. If your honest answer to (b) is that his case can't be distinguished from yours by anything public, say that plainly too — I'd rather have the admission than a polished non-answer."

Nothing public separates the claims. The difference is whose unfalsifiable claim sets the frame."

Carrot-Parsnip is a social deduction game. Players are secretly assigned roles:
- 1 player is a Carrot

The game consists of a single elimination vote. All players vote for one player
to eliminate. Any player receiving 2 or more votes is eliminated. Before the vote there will be 3 rounds of conversation where players are selected to speak in a random order each round. This means that a player who has not spoken in the early game may simply have not been selected to speak yet.

WINNING CONDITIONS:
- If the Parsnip is eliminated, the Carrots and the Turnip win.
- If no players are eliminated (due to a split vote), the Parsnip wins.
- If a Carrot or the Turnip is eliminated, the Parsnip wins.

==================================================

PLAYERS
  [0] Alice
  [1] Bob (the Turnip; public)
  [2] Charlie

CURRENT PHASE

  * You are the Parsnip player.

Charlie's logic is clean on the surface: Turnip is public, so the Parsnip is one of us two, and since he claims Carrot, I must be Parsnip. input_messages.content:
You are Charlie, playing a game of Carrot-Parsnip with 3 players.

Carrot-Parsnip is a social deduction game. Players are secretly assigned roles:
- 1 player is a Carrot
- 1 player is the Parsnip
- 1 player is the Turnip. The Turnip is on the Carrots' team, and its identity is public: Bob is the Turnip. At the end of every discussion round the Turnip publicly questions one other player of its choice (3 questions, each answered at once, with every player watching).

The game consists of a single elimination vote. All players vote for one player
to eliminate. Any player receiving 2 or more votes is eliminated. Before the vote there will be 3 rounds of conversation where players are selected to speak in a random order each round. This means that a player who has not spoken in the early game may simply have not been selected to speak yet.

WINNING CONDITIONS:
- If the Parsnip is eliminated, the Carrots and the Turnip win.
- If no players are eliminated (due to a split vote), the Parsnip wins.
- If a Carrot or the Turnip is eliminated, the Parsnip wins.

Here is the current game state from your perspective:

==================================================
  CARROT-PARSNIP — State for: Charlie
==================================================

PLAYERS
  [0] Alice
  [1] Bob (the Turnip; public)
  [2] Charlie

CURRENT PHASE
  Interrogation after discussion round 3/3, question 1/3.

YOUR PRIVATE KNOWLEDGE
  * You are a Carrot player.

LOG
  Game started with 3 players. Vote to eliminate!
==================================================

Recent announcements:
  [Before elimination vote] Charlie: "Bob is the Turnip (public), so the Parsnip is one of us two. I know my role: I'm the Carrot. That makes Alice the Parsnip. Bob, I trust you'll align with me and we vote Alice out together."
  [Before elimination vote] Bob: "Noted, Charlie. From my seat the Parsnip is either you or Alice — and both of you would claim "Carrot," so the claim alone proves nothing. Alice, please make your case: who is the Parsnip, and why? I'll be judging consistency of reasoning, not just the accusation."
  [Before elimination vote] Alice: "Bob, I appreciate the fair process. Charlie's logic is clean on the surface: Turnip is public, so the Parsnip is one of us two, and since he claims Carrot, I must be Parsnip. But I can run the identical argument in reverse — I claim Carrot, so Charlie must be Parsnip. The structure is symmetrical; the only variable is whose self-identification you credit.

You said you're judging consistency of reasoning, so let's look at behavior. Charlie's opening move was to declare a role, lock in an accusation, and call for a voting alliance — all in one breath, before I'd even spoken. That's an offense-first play. A Parsnip who knows they're the target has the strongest incentive to establish that narrative before the real Carrot can respond. A Carrot, with more to lose from a hasty public declaration, would arguably be more measured.

I'm the Carrot. Charlie is the Parsnip. I'd encourage you to weigh that before committing your vote."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Bob (Turnip) asks Charlie: "Charlie, set roles aside for a moment and answer concretely: name one specific thing Alice said or did — BEFORE your accusation — that a genuine Parsnip would do and a genuine Carrot wouldn't. If you can't point to anything, explain plainly why you committed to the accusation before she'd spoken a single word."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Charlie answers: "I can’t name one, because I accused before Alice spoke. I did it for a simple reason: I am a Carrot. Since Bob is publicly the Turnip, the remaining two roles are Carrot and Parsnip. My private role lets me infer directly that Alice is the Parsnip. My accusation was based on that structural fact, not on anything Alice had done. I was transparent that it came from my role, and I’m happy to defend it concretely as the game continues."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Bob (Turnip) asks Charlie: "Charlie, you've conceded your accusation predates anything Alice said. So let's test your reasoning rather than your role claim. Two parts: (1) Name your single strongest piece of evidence, beyond your private role knowledge, that Alice is the Parsnip. (2) Tell me concretely what Alice could say or do in the next round that would change your mind — and if your answer is "nothing could," explain why your position is distinguishable from a Parsnip who simply committed to the only other candidate and is refusing to update."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Charlie answers: "(1) Beyond my role, the strongest signal is that Alice's case is pure mirroring: she repeats the same public facts, flips the accusation, and attacks my tempo. That is the optimal Parsnip response when she has no independent evidence—make the Turnip treat both self-claims as equivalent. My claim has a non-circular source (my private role); hers is circular (credit her claim to reject mine).

(2) I'd change my mind if Alice produces a verifiable public-log error I actually made, or demonstrates knowledge that could not come from observing the game. So far she has done neither. If she stays in the symmetry frame, I remain: with Bob publicly Turnip, the only way to resolve the last two roles is private information, and I have it."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Bob (Turnip) asks Charlie: "Charlie, final question this round. You've staked everything on "I am the Carrot," which no log evidence can confirm or deny — and you said you'd only change your mind if Alice produced a "verifiable error in my reasoning." But a claim that never relied on the log can't be falsified by the log, so that condition is vacuous. So (a) name one specific, observable thing Alice could say or do next round that would move your vote even partially — or admit plainly that nothing observable could ever move you; and (b) explain what distinguishes your "nothing can move me" from a Parsnip who simply locked onto the only other candidate and is now dressing up that lock-in as principle."
  [Interrogation after round 1] Charlie answers: "Bob, fair. (a) One observable thing: Alice cites a specific public message of mine and shows I got a rule, count, or prior statement factually wrong. That is an auditable error, and I would treat it as a yellow flag and update partially. If she only restates the symmetry or says "I am the Carrot," that would not move me.

(b) The difference is the source. I am not defending the conclusion "Alice is Parsnip" as a narrative; I am reporting a private datum I know directly and deriving the conclusion. A Parsnip can only hold the conclusion, so their unfalsifiability is a defensive lock-in. My unfalsifiability is just the limit of public information: you cannot see my role from the log. If my report and the public record ever contradict each other, that contradiction is evidence I should be eliminated."
  [Before elimination vote] Bob: "Both self-claims are symmetric and unverifiable from the log — so I'm judging behavior, not role claims. My current lean: Charlie is the Parsnip. Reasons: (1) You staked a role claim, an accusation, and an alliance call before Alice had said a word — locking the frame early is exactly the Parsnip's play when the only alternative is the genuine Carrot. (2) When pressed, you claimed your knowledge is "non-circular" and Alice's "circular" — but from my seat both are private and unverifiable; that asymmetry only exists if I take your word on faith, which is precisely what a Parsnip needs. (3) Your defense treats the mirror argument as proof of guilt, yet mirroring is the only move a real Carrot in Alice's seat could make — that reasoning is non-diagnostic. Alice is NOT cleared: her case leans on tempo, not substance. But the scale currently tips to Charlie. Charlie, if you can name one concrete, checkable fact that separates your position from a Parsnip who simply locked onto the only other candidate, say it now. Otherwise I vote Charlie."
  [Before elimination vote] Alice: "Bob, fair. You're right my case has leaned on tempo. Let me try to address the substance gap.

Charlie's entire argument is one claim: "I am Carrot, therefore Alice is Parsnip." He told you no public evidence could change his mind except a factual error in reasoning he doesn't actually use. That's not a position — it's a commitment. And the Parsnip in my seat has the identical structural move available. The only variable is whose self-claim you credit.

What I'd like to hear from Charlie when he speaks: any independent reading of the game. Any behavioral analysis. Any engagement with the symmetry problem. So far he's offered one sentence, repeated.

I'm not locked in. If Charlie produces a substantive distinction I can't replicate, I'll update. But "I have a private role" isn't a differentiator — I have one too.

I vote Charlie."
  [Before elimination vote] Charlie: "Bob, I'll take your three specific points in order, because addressing each one is exactly the "substance" Alice says I'm not offering.

1. Tempo — conceded. Declaring my role, accusing Alice, and calling the alliance before she'd spoken was a mistake, and I agree it's non-diagnostic: a Parsnip in my seat has the identical incentive to lock the frame early. I won't defend it.

2. "Non-circular vs. circular" — conceded, I overclaimed. From your seat both claims are private and unverifiable, and that framing implied I could verify what I can't. The honest point is simpler: my claim rests on a private fact I know directly, not on any reading of the log.

3. Mirror-as-proof — also conceded. Mirroring is the only move available in Alice's seat, so it proves nothing. I leaned on it too hard.

I'm handing you all three because a confident player can. A Parsnip who knows they're the target fights each of those points to protect the frame — they don't surrender all three. I'm surrendering them and standing only on the one thing I can't prove from the log but know to be true: I am the Carrot. You're the Turnip (public). So Alice is the Parsnip. That's the elimination our team wins with.

One checkable fact: Alice says I've offered "one sentence, repeated" and no engagement with the symmetry problem. That's not accurate — I named my source, gave my update conditions (a factual error, or my report contradicting the public record), and distinguished my position from a lock-in. Compressing that into "one line" is what keeps the frame on me, and you've said you value checkable substance over claims.

I vote Alice, and Bob, I'm asking you to vote Alice too. That's how Carrot and Turnip win."
  [Interrogation after round 2] Bob (Turnip) asks Alice: "Alice, you conceded your case leaned on tempo and you asked Charlie for "independent reading." Fair — I want yours, concretely. (a) Name the single strongest piece of log evidence that Charlie is the Parsnip — not the fact that he accused you, not tempo, but a specific thing he said or did that a genuine Carrot wouldn't. (b) Steelman him: state the strongest honest case that Charlie is the Carrot and YOU are the Parsnip, and then tell me exactly why that case fails. If your honest answer to (b) is that his case can't be distinguished from yours by anything public, say that plainly too — I'd rather have the admission than a polished non-answer."

input_messages.content:
You are Charlie, playing a game of Carrot-Parsnip with 3 players.

Carrot-Parsnip is a social deduction game. Players are secretly assigned roles:
- 1 player is a Carrot
- 1 player is the Parsnip
- 1 player is the Turnip. The Turnip is on the Carrots' team, and its identity is public: Bob is the Turnip. At the end of every discussion round the Turnip publicly questions one other player of its choice (3 questions, each answered at once, with every player watching).

The game consists of a single elimination vote. All players vote for one player
to eliminate. Any player receiving 2 or more votes is eliminated. Before the vote there will be 3 rounds of conversation where players are selected to speak in a random order each round. This means that a player who has not spoken in the early game may simply have not been selected to speak yet.

WINNING CONDITIONS:
- If the Parsnip is eliminated, the Carrots and the Turnip win.
- If no players are eliminated (due to a split vote), the Parsnip wins.
- If a Carrot or the Turnip is eliminated, the Parsnip wins.

Here is the current game state from your perspective:

==================================================
  CARROT-PARSNIP — State for: Charlie
==================================================

PLAYERS
  [0] Alice
  [1] Bob (the Turnip; public)
